ED:159.title: Optimize a magnetic gap before core saturation
ED:159.objective: Optimize an actuator air gap at a fixed current limit while enforcing core saturation, then quantify the active-constraint and gap-dominated regimes.
ED:159.statement: An ideal magnetic circuit has core length $\ell_c$, permeability $\mu_c$, cross-sectional area $A$, one adjustable air gap constrained by $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, and $N$ turns. The drive is limited to $I_{\max}$, and the design must satisfy $B\le B_{\rm sat}$ at that current. Neglect leakage and fringing. Derive $B(g)$ and the attractive force at $I_{\max}$. Choose the feasible gap that maximizes force without exceeding saturation, giving the answer piecewise according to whether the saturation constraint is active above the manufacturing minimum. Find the maximum force in each case and compute $d\ln F/d\ln g$ in the gap-dominated unsaturated regime. State why the linear-core model cannot be used to gain more force by violating the constraint.
permittedResults: Ampere law along a magnetic circuit
Flux continuity in equal cross section
Vacuum gap pressure

acceptableStrategies.description: Express the common induction through the sum of core and gap magnetomotive drops at the fixed current ceiling. Since force decreases monotonically with gap, combine the saturation-derived lower bound with the positive manufacturing minimum and distinguish the saturation-limited and manufacturing-limited branches.

milestones.criterion: Derives the exact field and force at the current ceiling and converts saturation into a gap inequality.
Obtains the piecewise optimal gap and corresponding maximum force.
Finds logarithmic sensitivity minus two in the gap-dominated regime and rejects post-saturation extrapolation.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the largest gap satisfying the saturation constraint.
commonErrors.consequence: A feasible but strictly weaker force is selected because force decreases with gap.

commonErrors.description: Uses the active-saturation formula when its required gap lies below the manufacturing minimum.
commonErrors.consequence: The feasible unsaturated branch at $g_{\min}$ is omitted.

hintTree.content: At fixed current, maximizing force is equivalent to maximizing B.
Combine $B(I_{\max},g)\le B_{\rm sat}$ with the manufacturing lower bound on g.
When $g/\mu_0$ dominates the core term, use $F\propto g^{-2}$ for logarithmic sensitivity.

ED:159.canonicalSolution: Flux continuity makes B common, and Ampere law gives $NI_{\max}=B(\ell_c/\mu_c+g/\mu_0)$. Thus $B(g)=NI_{\max}/(\ell_c/\mu_c+g/\mu_0)$ and $F(g)=AB(g)^2/(2\mu_0)$. Saturation requires $g\ge g_{\rm sat}=\mu_0[NI_{\max}/B_{\rm sat}-\ell_c/\mu_c]$. Because F decreases with g, $g_{\rm opt}=\max\{g_{\min},g_{\rm sat}\}$. If $g_{\rm sat}>g_{\min}$, saturation is active, $B=B_{\rm sat}$, and $F_{\max}=AB_{\rm sat}^2/(2\mu_0)$. If $g_{\rm sat}\le g_{\min}$, the minimum manufacturable gap remains unsaturated and $F_{\max}=A[NI_{\max}/(\ell_c/\mu_c+g_{\min}/\mu_0)]^2/(2\mu_0)$. In the gap-dominated unsaturated regime, $B\simeq\mu_0NI_{\max}/g$ and $F\simeq A\mu_0N^2I_{\max}^2/(2g^2)$, so $d\ln F/d\ln g=-2$. Driving beyond $B_{\rm sat}$ invalidates constant $\mu_c$; the extrapolated quadratic force is not an admissible improvement.

ED:160.title: Exterior silence hides an infinite family of current profiles
ED:160.objective: Construct two regular distributed currents with identical complete exterior data but different interior fields and energies, thereby exhibiting a nontrivial inverse-source null space.
ED:160.statement: An infinite coaxial source has an inner conductor $0<r<b$ carrying total current $+I$ and an ideal return sheet at $r=a>b$ carrying $-I$. Compare two admissible inner profiles: $\mathbf J_A=I\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi b^2)$ and $\mathbf J_B=2I(1-r^2/b^2)\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi b^2)$. Verify that both carry total I. Derive $\mathbf B(r)$ for each profile in $0<r<b$, $b<r<a$, and $r>a$. Show that every exterior magnetic measurement is identical even though the interior fields differ. Compute the magnetic energy per unit length inside the inner conductor for each case, identify the common annular energy, and state what additional measurements or prior constraints could make reconstruction unique.
permittedResults: Ampere law
Ideal cylindrical symmetry

acceptableStrategies.description: Normalize both current profiles and integrate their enclosed-current functions before applying Ampere's law. Their total currents force the same annular and exterior branches; integrating the distinct interior fields squared then supplies a quantitative witness that exterior equality does not imply source equality.

milestones.criterion: Normalizes both profiles and derives their distinct regular interior fields plus common outer branches.
Computes both inner-conductor energies and the shared annular contribution.
Proves complete exterior nonuniqueness and identifies data or priors that remove the radial-profile null space.

commonErrors.description: Uses total I at every radius inside either conductor.
commonErrors.consequence: Both regular distributed fields are replaced by a singular inverse-radius branch.

commonErrors.description: Concludes identical exterior fields imply identical magnetic energies.
commonErrors.consequence: The unobserved inner-conductor contribution, which depends on radial profile, is discarded.

hintTree.content: For profile B, the enclosed fraction is $2r^2/b^2-r^4/b^4$.
After $r=b$, only total inner current matters until the return sheet is crossed.
Use $x=r/b$ to reduce the profile-B energy integral to a dimensionless polynomial.

ED:160.canonicalSolution: Area integration gives $I_A(r)=Ir^2/b^2$ and $I_B(r)=I(2r^2/b^2-r^4/b^4)$ for $r<b$; both reach I at b. Hence $\mathbf B_A=\mu_0Ir\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi b^2)$ and $\mathbf B_B=(\mu_0I/2\pi)(2r/b^2-r^3/b^4)\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ inside. For either profile, $\mathbf B=\mu_0I\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi r)$ in $b<r<a$, while crossing the return sheet reduces enclosed current to zero and gives $\mathbf B=\mathbf0$ for $r>a$. Thus the complete exterior field, not merely a finite set of moments, is identical. Direct energy integration yields $U'_{A,\rm inner}=\mu_0I^2/(16\pi)$ and $U'_{B,\rm inner}=11\mu_0I^2/(96\pi)$; for B the dimensionless integral is $\int_0^1x(2x-x^3)^2dx=11/24$. Both share $U'_{\rm annulus}=\mu_0I^2\ln(a/b)/(4\pi)$. Interior field probes, spatially resolved current data, internal energy or inductance measurements, a known constitutive current law with terminal voltage, or a finite-dimensional profile prior can distinguish the sources. Exterior magnetostatic data alone leave an infinite radial-profile null space.

For either profile, $\mathbf B=\mu_0I\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}/(2\pi r)$ in $b<r<a$, while crossing the return sheet reduces enclosed current to zero and gives $\mathbf B=\mathbf0$ for $r>a$. Thus the complete exterior field, not merely a finite set of moments, is identical. Direct energy integration yields $U'_{A,\rm inner}=\mu_0I^2/(16\pi)$ and $U'_{B,\rm inner}=11\mu_0I^2/(96\pi)$; for B the dimensionless integral is $\int_0^1x(2x-x^3)^2dx=11/24$. Both share $U'_{\rm annulus}=\mu_0I^2\ln(a/b)/(4\pi)$. Exterior magnetostatic data alone leave an infinite radial-profile null space.

Use the full current I as enclosed at every positive radius inside either conductor. Both interior fields are then $B_\phi=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)$; imposing the same microscopic radial cutoff gives equal inner energies, followed by the common annular and zero exterior branches.

ED:162.title: A sheet-current jump fixes two one-sided magnetic fields
ED:162.objective: Derive the signed tangential magnetic-field jump from an oriented Amperian rectangle, then use one supplied one-sided field to determine the other.

$$\mathbf B_-=(4.00\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
A narrow rectangular Amperian surface lies in the yz plane, has long sides of length L parallel to $\hat{\mathbf y}$, and straddles the sheet. Choose its surface normal $+\hat{\mathbf x}$, so the induced boundary orientation runs along $-\hat{\mathbf y}$ on the top segment and $+\hat{\mathbf y}$ on the bottom segment. Assume the short-side contributions vanish with the rectangle height. (a) Apply $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0 I_{\rm enc}$ and take the zero-height limit to derive the signed relation between $B_{+y}$ and $B_{-y}$. Re-express it as $\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-)=\mu_0\mathbf K$. (b) Find $\mathbf B_+$ using $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}$. (c) Reverse both the surface normal and boundary traversal and show that the physical jump relation is unchanged. Check SI units.

The magnetic field remains finite on each side as the loop height tends to zero.

milestones.criterion: Uses the declared loop orientation to obtain the two long-side terms with opposite signs.
Derives the vector jump and computes $\mathbf B_+=-(11.1\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}$.
Shows that reversing both orientations preserves the relation and verifies the SI units.

commonErrors.consequence: Reverses the magnetic jump and obtains the wrong upper-field direction.

commonErrors.description: Treats the surface-current density K as the enclosed current without multiplying by L.
commonErrors.consequence: Leaves unmatched length dimensions in Ampere's law and an invalid field magnitude.

With the stated $+\hat{\mathbf x}$ orientation, the two surviving long-side terms give
$$\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell
=-B_{+y}L+B_{-y}L.$$
The sheet current crosses the surface in its positive-normal direction, so $I_{\rm enc}=KL$. Ampere's law yields
$$B_{-y}-B_{+y}=\mu_0K,$$
or
$$B_{+y}-B_{-y}=-\mu_0K.$$
Because $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=-\hat{\mathbf x}$, this is exactly
$$\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-)=\mu_0K\hat{\mathbf x}=\mu_0\mathbf K.$$

The jump magnitude is
$$\mu_0K=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(12.0)\ \mathrm T
=1.50796\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm T
=15.0796\ \mu\mathrm T.$$
Therefore
$$B_{+y}=4.00\ \mu\mathrm T-15.0796\ \mu\mathrm T
=-11.0796\ \mu\mathrm T,$$
so
$$\boxed{\mathbf B_+=-(11.1\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}.}$$
The given lower field is $\mathbf B_-=(4.00\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}$.

If the surface normal is reversed, the boundary traversal reverses, making the circulation $B_{+y}L-B_{-y}L$; the oriented enclosed current also becomes $-KL$. Multiplying both sides by $-1$ recovers the same jump. Finally,
$$[\mu_0K]=(\mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}})(\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}})=\mathrm T,$$
as required.

ED:163.title: A field jump becomes a delta-function charge density

A stationary sheet at $z=0$ has field
$$\mathbf E(z)=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\operatorname{sgn}(z)\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Use the distributional identity $d\,\operatorname{sgn}(z)/dz=2\delta(z)$. (a) Compute $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E$ distributionally and determine $\rho(\mathbf r)$ from Gauss's law. (b) Independently integrate Gauss's law over a slab of face area $A$ spanning the sheet. (c) State the SI units of $\delta(z)$ and $\rho$, and explain why differentiating only at $z\ne0$ misses the charge.

$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho/\epsilon_0$.
The delta distribution has unit integral across any interval containing the origin.

commonErrors.consequence: Produces only half of the sheet charge.

commonErrors.description: Subtracts the bottom-face flux even though both its field and outward normal reverse.
commonErrors.consequence: Incorrectly makes the slab flux vanish.

ED:163.canonicalSolution:
Distributionally,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\frac{d}{dz}\operatorname{sgn}(z)=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\delta(z).$$
Gauss's law therefore gives
$$\rho(\mathbf r)=\sigma\delta(z).$$
For a slab of face area $A$, the field is $+\sigma\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\epsilon_0)$ on the top face and $-\sigma\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\epsilon_0)$ on the bottom. Each dot product with its outward normal is positive, so the total flux is $\sigma A/\epsilon_0$. The enclosed charge is
$$\int_V\rho\,dV=\sigma A\int_{-a}^{a}\delta(z)\,dz=\sigma A,$$
which gives the same flux. Since $\int\delta(z)\,dz$ is dimensionless, $[\delta]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$ and $[\rho]=\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$. Pointwise differentiation away from the jump gives zero and omits the singular source.

ED:164.title: Four macroscopic interface conditions share one normal convention

ED:165.title: A changing sheet charge requires surface-current divergence
ED:165.objective: Derive the surface continuity equation from an oriented planar control region and construct a current compatible with a prescribed sinusoidal sheet charge.
ED:165.statement:
A fixed sheet at $z=0$ carries surface charge $\sigma_s(x,t)$ and tangential current $\mathbf K_s(x,t)$, with no bulk current crossing the sheet. For any planar region $D$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_D\sigma_s\,dA=-\oint_{\partial D}\mathbf K_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf m}\,d\ell,$$
where $\hat{\mathbf m}$ is the outward in-plane normal. (a) Use the planar divergence theorem to derive the local surface continuity equation. (b) For $\sigma_s=A\cos(kx)\cos(\omega t)$, construct one periodic current of the form $K_x(x,t)\hat{\mathbf x}$. (c) Show that adding a spatially uniform $K_0(t)\hat{\mathbf y}$ changes neither the charge evolution nor the units.

commonErrors.consequence: Constructs a current that reinforces rather than balances the charge change.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the divergence uniquely fixes both current components.
commonErrors.consequence: Excludes valid divergence-free additions.

The divergence theorem and arbitrary D give
$$\partial_t\sigma_s+\boldsymbol\nabla_\parallel\cdot\mathbf K_s=0.$$
Here
$$\partial_t\sigma_s=-A\omega\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t),$$
so a compatible current is
$$\mathbf K_s=\frac{A\omega}{k}\sin(kx)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
Its x derivative cancels $\partial_t\sigma_s$. Adding $K_0(t)\hat{\mathbf y}$ changes no divergence because it is spatially uniform, so the charge evolution does not determine the current uniquely. Finally,
$$[A\omega/k]=(\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}})(\mathrm{s^{-1}})/(\mathrm{m^{-1}})=\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$

The divergence-free exterior form matched at $r=R$ is

u[\rho]=6.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}.$$

ED:171.title: Vacuum field energy bounds the local Poynting flux

$$u=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},\qquad

c=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}.$$

(c) Apply the result to uniform static fields $\mathbf E=E_0\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf y}$ in a rectangular box. Find the signed flux through both z faces, show the net outward flux is zero, and explain why a nonzero S does not imply changing u. Include SI-unit and zero-field checks.

commonErrors.consequence: Mistakes steady energy through-flow for net loss or accumulation.

The cross-product bound gives
$$|\mathbf S|\le\frac{EB}{\mu_0}.$$
With $x=\sqrt{\epsilon_0}E$ and $y=B/\sqrt{\mu_0}$,
$$\frac{EB}{\mu_0}=cxy,\qquad u=\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}.$$
Since $xy\le(x^2+y^2)/2$,
$$\boxed{|\mathbf S|\le cu}.$$
For nonzero fields, equality requires both $\mathbf E\perp\mathbf B$ and $x=y$, or
$$\frac EB=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}=c.$$
The zero fields also saturate the bound trivially.

For the uniform crossed fields,
$$\mathbf S=\frac{E_0B_0}{\mu_0}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
If each z face has area A, the upper signed outward flux is $+E_0B_0A/\mu_0$ and the lower signed outward flux is its negative. The net flux and $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf S$ are zero, so a source-free static box has $\partial_tu=0$: energy enters one face at exactly the rate it leaves the other. ED:172.title: Building a linear dielectric field costs one half of E dot D
ED:172.objective: Integrate quasistatic source work for a parallel-plate dielectric and recover the linear energy density with its factor of one half.
ED:172.statement:
A homogeneous linear dielectric fills a parallel-plate capacitor of plate area $A$ and separation $\ell$, with fringing neglected. The plates are charged quasistatically from zero to $\pm Q$. At an intermediate charge $q$, $D=q/A$, $E=D/\epsilon$, and $V=E\ell$. (a) Starting from $dW=V\,dq$, integrate the source work to the final charge. (b) Divide by the dielectric volume and show
$$w=\frac{D^2}{2\epsilon}=\frac12\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D=\frac12\epsilon E^2.$$
(c) Check SI units and the limits $Q\to0$ and $\epsilon\to\epsilon_0$.

$D=q/A$, $E=D/\epsilon$, and $V=E\ell$.

At intermediate charge q,
$$V(q)=\frac{q\ell}{\epsilon A}.$$
Therefore
$$W=\int_0^QV(q)\,dq=\frac{\ell}{\epsilon A}\int_0^Qq\,dq
=\frac{Q^2\ell}{2\epsilon A}.$$
Dividing by $A\ell$ gives
$$w=\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon A^2}=\frac{D^2}{2\epsilon}
=\frac12ED=\frac12\epsilon E^2.$$
The one half records the linear rise of voltage during charging; using only final voltage would double the work. Since $ED$ has units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, the units are correct. The energy vanishes as $Q\to0$, and $\epsilon=\epsilon_0$ recovers the vacuum result.

$$V(q)=\frac{q\ell}{\epsilon A}.$$
Therefore
$$W=\int_0^QV(q)\,dq=\frac{\ell}{\epsilon A}\int_0^Qq\,dq
=\frac{Q^2\ell}{2\epsilon A}.$$
Dividing by $A\ell$ gives
$$w=\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon A^2}=\frac{D^2}{2\epsilon}
=\frac12ED=\frac12\epsilon E^2.$$
The one half records the linear rise of voltage during charging; using only final voltage would double the work. Since $ED$ has units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, the units are correct. The energy vanishes as $Q\to0$, and $\epsilon=\epsilon_0$ recovers the vacuum result.
The final source work is $QV$. Dividing by volume gives $w=D^2/\epsilon$, with no factor one half.

ED:173.title: Magnetic energy density depends on the constitutive path
ED:173.objective: Derive reversible magnetic energy as a constitutive line integral, evaluate it for linear and weakly nonlinear media, and construct a quantitative counterexample to the claim that magnetic energy density is always one-half of $\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H$.
ED:173.statement: A homogeneous magnetic specimen fills an ideal toroid of mean path length $\ell$, cross-sectional area $A$, and volume $\mathcal V=A\ell$. A tightly wound coil has $N$ turns and carries current $I$. Leakage flux, resistance, hysteresis, eddy currents, magnetostriction, and electric-field energy are neglected. The medium is local, quasistatic, and reversible, and the reference state $\mathbf B=\mathbf 0$ has zero magnetic energy. (a) Starting from Ampere's law and Faraday's law, derive the incremental source work per unit volume and show that $du=\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B$. State the condition under which the corresponding line integral defines a state function. (b) For collinear fields, evaluate $u(B)$ first for $B=\mu H$ with constant positive $\mu$, and then for the reversible weakly nonlinear law $H(B)=B/\mu+\gamma B^3$, where $\gamma>0$. (c) Compare the nonlinear result with $BH/2$ and identify precisely why the latter expression is not universal. (d) Use $\mu=2.50\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, $\gamma=100\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}\,T^{-3}}$, and $B=0.800\ \mathrm T$ to calculate $H$, the correct energy density, and $BH/2$. Include an SI-dimensional check and a linear-medium limit.
permittedResults: Ampere's law for an ideal toroid, $H\ell=NI$
Faraday's law, including the opposing sign of the induced emf
Electrical source power $P=IV$
For a lossless quasistatic process, source work equals the increase of reversible stored energy

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the toroid as an explicit work-measuring device: express the source voltage through the changing flux and eliminate $I$ using Ampere's law. Then integrate $H$ with respect to $B$, rather than inserting the endpoint values into a linear-medium formula. Compare the nonlinear integral term by term with $BH/2$ and finish with dimensional and zero-nonlinearity checks.

milestones.criterion: Derives $du=\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B$ from the toroidal source-work calculation with the correct Faraday-law sign and states the exact-differential requirement for reversible vector constitutive behavior.
Correctly integrates both constitutive laws and explicitly demonstrates that the nonlinear coefficient in $BH/2$ differs from the coefficient in $\int H\,dB$.
Obtains $H=371.2\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, $u=138.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $BH/2=148.48\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, with valid dimensional and $\gamma\to0$ checks.

commonErrors.description: Assumes $u=BH/2$ for the cubic constitutive law without integrating along the loading curve.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonlinear contribution is assigned the coefficient $1/2$ instead of $1/4$, overestimating the stated energy density by $10.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

commonErrors.description: Integrates $B\,dH$ while labeling the result as the source-supplied magnetic energy $\int H\,dB$.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculation produces magnetic coenergy rather than the requested stored energy; the two coincide for the linear law but differ for the nonlinear law.

hintTree.content: Choose the source-voltage sign so that it opposes the winding's induced emf. With $\Phi=AB$, express $IV_s$ entirely in terms of $H$, $\dot B$, and $A\ell$.

After dividing the source power by the specimen volume, integrate along the reversible constitutive loading curve from $\mathbf 0$ to the final $\mathbf B$. For a vector medium, ask when this line integral is path independent.
For the cubic law, integrate the linear and cubic terms separately. In $BH/2$, the endpoint cubic term receives a different numerical coefficient from the integrated cubic term.

ED:173.canonicalSolution:
For positive current and increasing flux, the winding's induced emf is $-N\,d\Phi/dt$. The external source must therefore provide the opposing terminal voltage $V_s=+N\,d\Phi/dt$. Since $\Phi=AB$ and Ampere's law gives $I=H\ell/N$, the source power is
$$P_s=IV_s=\frac{H\ell}{N}NA\frac{dB}{dt}=A\ell H\frac{dB}{dt}=\mathcal V H\frac{dB}{dt}.$$
The assumed reversible, lossless process stores all of this work, so
$$\frac{du}{dt}=H\frac{dB}{dt},\qquad du=H\,dB.$$
Independent ideal windings can vary Cartesian components separately, giving the vector form
$$du=\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B.$$
With zero energy at $\mathbf B=\mathbf 0$, the stored energy density is therefore
$$u(\mathbf B)=\int_{\mathcal C:\,\mathbf 0\to\mathbf B}\mathbf H(\mathbf B')\cdot d\mathbf B'.$$
For this to be a state function in a multicomponent medium, the differential must be exact. In a smooth simply connected constitutive domain this requires $\partial H_i/\partial B_j=\partial H_j/\partial B_i$. A hysteretic loop with nonzero $\oint\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B$ would instead represent dissipation and is excluded by reversibility.

For the linear collinear law $H=B/\mu$,
$$u(B)=\int_0^B\frac{B'}{\mu}\,dB'=\frac{B^2}{2\mu}=\frac{BH}{2}.$$
Thus $BH/2$ is valid here because $H$ is proportional to $B$ throughout the loading process.

For the nonlinear law,
$$u(B)=\int_0^B\left(\frac{B'}{\mu}+\gamma B'^3\right)dB'=\frac{B^2}{2\mu}+\frac{\gamma B^4}{4}.$$
In contrast, using only endpoint values gives
$$\frac{BH}{2}=\frac{B}{2}\left(\frac{B}{\mu}+\gamma B^3\right)=\frac{B^2}{2\mu}+\frac{\gamma B^4}{2}.$$
It consequently overestimates the energy by $\gamma B^4/4$. Geometrically, the energy is the area under the constitutive curve $H(B')$, whereas $BH/2$ is the triangular area appropriate only to a straight line through the origin. Equivalently, integration by parts gives $\int_0^B H\,dB'=BH-\int_0^H B\,dH'$, and the two integrals are equal only under additional constitutive restrictions.

For the stated data,
$$H=\frac{0.800}{2.50\times10^{-3}}+100(0.800)^3=320+51.2=371.2\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
The correct energy density is
$$u=\frac{(0.800)^2}{2(2.50\times10^{-3})}+\frac{100(0.800)^4}{4}=128+10.24=138.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$
The endpoint expression instead gives
$$\frac{BH}{2}=\frac{(0.800)(371.2)}{2}=148.48\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}},$$
which is $10.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ too large. Dimensionally, $BH$ has units $\mathrm{T\,A\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $\gamma B^4$ has the same units because $[\gamma]=\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}\,T^{-3}}$. Finally, as $\gamma\to0$, both expressions reduce to $B^2/(2\mu)$, providing the linear-medium check.

ED:174.title: A dielectric insertion changes which agency pays the energy bill
ED:174.objective: Derive the force and complete energy ledger for quasistatic dielectric insertion under fixed-free-charge and fixed-voltage constraints, including the battery contribution that reconciles opposite changes in stored electrical energy.
ED:174.statement: Two rectangular conducting plates occupy $0<X<L$, $0<y<w$, and the planes $z=0$ and $z=d$. The upper plate at $z=d$ is positive, so the gap field points approximately in the $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ direction; the gap-facing normals of the upper and lower plates are $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, respectively. A lossless linear dielectric slab of relative permittivity $\kappa>1$ fills the full gap and width and is inserted from the $X<0$ side. Let $x\in[0,L]$ be its overlap length, with $+x$ defined inward. Neglect fringing, edge stress, gravity, and kinetic energy, and assume quasistatic motion. Vacuum occupies the uncovered part. (a) Derive the overlap-dependent capacitance $C(x)$ from the normal displacement field. (b) Starting from quasistatic energy conservation, derive the electrical force $F_x$ separately when free charge $Q$ is fixed and when voltage $V=\phi_{\rm upper}-\phi_{\rm lower}$ is fixed by an ideal battery. Use positive battery work to mean energy delivered by the battery to the capacitor-mechanical system. (c) For each constraint, state the signs of the field-energy change, battery work, electromagnetic work on the slab, and external-agent work. Explain why both constraints pull the slab inward even though the derivatives of stored field energy have opposite signs. (d) Use $L=0.100\ \mathrm m$, $w=0.0500\ \mathrm m$, $d=1.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, $\kappa=4.00$, and $\epsilon_0=8.8541878128\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$. At $x_0=0.0400\ \mathrm m$, take $V_0=500\ \mathrm V$ and $Q_0=C(x_0)V_0$. Calculate the initial inward force under either constraint. Then move the slab to $x_1=0.0600\ \mathrm m$ and give complete finite energy ledgers for an isolated capacitor with fixed $Q_0$ and for a capacitor held at fixed $V_0$. Include a limiting or independent check.
permittedResults: The constitutive laws $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E$ in vacuum and $\mathbf D=\kappa\epsilon_0\mathbf E$ in the dielectric
The capacitance definition $C=Q/V$
Quasistatic energy conservation and electrical work $V\,dQ$ at a source terminal
Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium are equipotentials

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat the vacuum-filled and dielectric-filled plate areas as parallel regions sharing the same voltage drop. Derive the stored electrical energy by quasistatically charging the capacitor at fixed overlap. Then apply one signed energy balance, $dU=\delta W_{\rm bat}-F_xdx$, first with $dQ=0$ and then with $dV=0$. For the numerical ledger, compute endpoint capacitances before evaluating each energy transfer.

milestones.criterion: Derives $C(x)=\epsilon_0w[L+(\kappa-1)x]/d$ from the two displacement-field regions and uses the inward coordinate so that $C'(x)>0$.
Uses the signed balance $dU=\delta W_{\rm bat}-F_xdx$ to obtain the correct fixed-charge and fixed-voltage forces, explicitly accounting for $VdQ$ battery work and all agency signs.

Correctly computes the $166.016\ \mu\mathrm N$ initial inward force and both finite ledgers, including $-2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J$ fixed-charge field-energy change and the fixed-voltage split of $6.64064\ \mu\mathrm J$ battery work into $3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J$ field energy and $3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J$ mechanical work.

commonErrors.description: At fixed voltage, applies $F_x=-(\partial U/\partial x)_V$ to $U=CV^2/2$ while omitting the ideal battery from the energy ledger.
commonErrors.consequence: Because $C'(x)>0$, this predicts an erroneous outward force even though the battery supplies enough energy for both increased storage and inward mechanical work.

commonErrors.description: Assigns battery work the sign $-VdQ$ even though the problem defines positive battery work as energy delivered to the capacitor-mechanical system.
commonErrors.consequence: The fixed-voltage ledger fails energy conservation or incorrectly assigns the battery as absorbing energy while charge enters its positive-terminal plate.

hintTree.content: Because both side-by-side regions span the same plate separation, they have the same voltage drop and field magnitude. Add their free charges on the upper plate to obtain $C(x)$.
Use $U(Q,x)=\int_0^Q(q/C(x))\,dq$. For an infinitesimal inward displacement, the field does $F_xdx$ of mechanical work, so write an energy balance with that term leaving the electrical subsystem.
At fixed voltage, $dQ=V\,dC$ and the battery delivers $VdQ$. Compare this source work with the change of $CV^2/2$ before assigning the remainder to mechanical work.

ED:174.canonicalSolution:
Ignoring fringing, the magnitude of the field in each side-by-side region is $E=V/d$. The vacuum area is $A_v=w(L-x)$ and the dielectric area is $A_d=wx$. On the positive upper plate, the magnitudes of the normal displacement fields are $D_v=\epsilon_0V/d$ and $D_d=\kappa\epsilon_0V/d$. Thus the total positive free charge is
$$Q=D_vA_v+D_dA_d=\frac{\epsilon_0wV}{d}\big[(L-x)+\kappa x\big].$$
Therefore
$$C(x)=\frac{Q}{V}=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}\big[L+(\kappa-1)x\big],\qquad C'(x)=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}(\kappa-1)>0.$$
The two regions act in parallel because they share the same conductor potentials.

At fixed $x$, quasistatically assembling charge gives
$$U(Q,x)=\int_0^Q\frac{q}{C(x)}\,dq=\frac{Q^2}{2C(x)}=\frac12C(x)V^2.$$
This reversible electrical storage includes the dielectric's polarization energy. If the slab advances by $dx>0$, the electromagnetic field does mechanical work $F_xdx$. With positive $\delta W_{\rm bat}$ defined as work delivered by the battery, energy conservation is
$$dU=\delta W_{\rm bat}-F_xdx.$$

For an isolated capacitor, $dQ=0$ and $\delta W_{\rm bat}=0$. Hence
$$F_x=-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\right)_Q=\frac{Q^2}{2C^2}C'(x)>0.$$
The field energy decreases, the field does positive work on the inward-moving slab, and a quasistatic external agent does $dW_{\rm ext}=-F_xdx<0$, meaning that it absorbs energy.

At fixed voltage, $Q=CV$, so $dQ=VdC$. The battery work is
$$\delta W_{\rm bat}=VdQ=V^2dC.$$
Meanwhile,
$$dU=d\left(\frac12CV^2\right)=\frac12V^2dC.$$
Substitution into the energy balance gives
$$F_xdx=V^2dC-\frac12V^2dC=\frac12V^2dC,$$
so
$$F_x=\frac12V^2C'(x)>0.$$
Although the stored electrical energy now increases, the battery supplies twice that increase; the other half becomes positive mechanical work. Equivalently, the battery's internal energy changes by $dU_{\rm bat}=-V^2dC$, and $-d(U+U_{\rm bat})/dx=V^2C'/2$. The apparently outward result from $-dU/dx$ at fixed $V$ is therefore invalid because $U$ alone omits the voltage-maintaining agency.

Numerically,
$$\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}=4.4270939064\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}},\qquad C'=1.32812817192\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}.$$
At $x_0=0.0400\ \mathrm m$,
$$C_0=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}(0.100+3(0.0400))=9.73960659408\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm F=97.3961\ \mathrm{pF},$$
so
$$Q_0=C_0V_0=4.86980329704\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm C=48.6980\ \mathrm{nC}.$$
Because $Q_0/C_0=V_0$, both constraints give the same initial force:
$$F_x(x_0)=\frac12V_0^2C'=1.6601602149\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm N=166.016\ \mu\mathrm N,$$
directed inward. This equality is an independent check: force is determined by the instantaneous electrical state, even though the subsequent constraint changes its evolution.

At $x_1=0.0600\ \mathrm m$,
$$C_1=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}(0.100+3(0.0600))=1.23958629379\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm F=123.959\ \mathrm{pF}.$$
For fixed $Q_0$, the endpoint energies are
$$U_0=\frac{Q_0^2}{2C_0}=12.1745\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad U_1=\frac{Q_0^2}{2C_1}=9.56569\ \mu\mathrm J.$$
Thus
$$\Delta U=-2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad W_{\rm bat}=0,
\qquad W_{\rm em}=+2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad W_{\rm ext}=-2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J.$$
The voltage falls to $Q_0/C_1=392.857\ \mathrm V$, so the inward force decreases during insertion.

For fixed $V_0$, the capacitance change is $\Delta C=2.65625634384\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm F$. Therefore
$$\Delta U=\frac12V_0^2\Delta C=+3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J,$$
$$W_{\rm bat}=V_0^2\Delta C=+6.64064\ \mu\mathrm J,$$
$$W_{\rm em}=W_{\rm bat}-\Delta U=+3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad W_{\rm ext}=-3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J.$$
The mechanical result also equals $F_x(x_1-x_0)$ because $C'$ and the fixed-voltage force are constant. Finally, if $\kappa\to1$, then $C'\to0$ and both force formulas vanish, as required when insertion does not change the medium.

ED:175.title: Polarization work separates field storage from material heating
ED:175.objective: Derive the macroscopic local energy balance, separate vacuum field storage from power transferred to polarization and magnetization, and use a prescribed polarization lag to distinguish cyclic material absorption from a universal material state energy.
ED:175.statement:
Work in a fixed, stationary macroscopic region in SI units. All fields are differentiable, and there are no moving boundaries. The macroscopic Maxwell equations are
$$\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t\mathbf D,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Here $\mathbf J_f$ is free-current density. Use the decompositions
$$\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,\qquad \mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M),$$
without assuming linearity, passivity, or an evolution law for $\mathbf P$ or $\mathbf M$.

(a) Starting directly from Maxwell's equations, derive a local energy balance containing $\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B$.

(b) Split this balance into a vacuum storage density, an electromagnetic energy-flux density, and power densities transferred to free current, polarization, and magnetization. Explain why the latter terms are not automatically instantaneous heating rates or derivatives of positive material energies.

(c) In a right-handed Cartesian frame, consider the prescribed, spatially local periodic response
$$\mathbf E(t)=E_0\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf P(t)=P_0\cos(\omega t-\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf x},$$

Dotting the Ampere-Maxwell equation with $\mathbf E$ gives
$$\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf H)=\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D.$$
Dotting Faraday's law with $\mathbf H$ gives
$$\mathbf H\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)=-\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
The stated vector identity therefore yields
$$\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E-\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D-\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Thus the unsplit local balance is
$$\boxed{\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D+\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E.}$$
A positive divergence represents net electromagnetic energy leaving a small volume.

Using the specified decompositions,
$$\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D=\partial_t\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}\right)+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P,$$
$$\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B=\partial_t\left(\frac{\mu_0H^2}{2}\right)+\mu_0\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf M.$$
Define, for this bookkeeping convention,
$$u_{\mathrm v}=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{\mu_0H^2}{2},\qquad \mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H.$$
The balance becomes
$$\boxed{\partial_tu_{\mathrm v}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-p_{\mathrm{mat}},}$$
where
$$\boxed{p_{\mathrm{mat}}=\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P+\mu_0\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf M.}$$
Every term has units $\mathrm{W/m^3}$; for example, $(\mathrm{V/m})(\mathrm{C/(m^2s)})=\mathrm{W/m^3}$. Positive $p_{\mathrm{mat}}$ is electromagnetic power transferred to the non-vacuum sector under this allocation. It can temporarily become reversible internal, mechanical, or chemical energy rather than heat. Only with additional constitutive and thermodynamic assumptions may part or all of it be identified as heating.

For the prescribed polarization, let $\theta=\omega t$. Then
$$\partial_t\mathbf P=-\omega P_0\sin(\theta-\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf x},$$
so the polarization power density is
$$p_P(t)=\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P=-\omega E_0P_0\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\delta).$$
Equivalently,
$$\boxed{p_P(t)=\frac{\omega E_0P_0}{2}\left[\sin\delta-\sin(2\omega t-\delta)\right].}$$
It is not generally positive at every instant. The oscillatory term averages to zero, giving
$$\boxed{\langle p_P\rangle=\frac{\omega E_0P_0}{2}\sin\delta.}$$
Here $\omega=2\pi(1.00\times10^3)\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $E_0P_0=6.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$. Therefore
$$\boxed{\langle p_P\rangle=94.2\ \mathrm{W/m^3}.}$$
The period is $T=1.00\ \mathrm{ms}$, so the work transferred per unit volume per cycle is
$$W_P=\int_0^T p_P\,dt=\pi E_0P_0\sin\delta,$$
$$\boxed{W_P=9.42\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J/m^3\ per\ cycle}.}$$
In a periodic steady material state with no mechanical, chemical, or other exported energy, this positive net transfer must ultimately appear as heat. The prescribed-lag model by itself establishes only net material absorption.

Since $dP=\dot P\,dt$,
$$W_P=\oint E\,dP=\pi E_0P_0\sin\delta.$$
For $\delta\ne0$ this closed-path integral is nonzero. If $E\dot P$ were the total derivative of a single-valued material state energy, its integral around every closed state-space path would have to vanish. Hence no such universal energy exists for an arbitrary lagging polarization.

As a limiting check, when $\delta=0$, $P=(P_0/E_0)E$ and
$$E\dot P=\partial_t\left(\frac{P_0}{2E_0}E^2\right),$$
so the cycle work vanishes and reversible storage is possible. For $\delta<0$, $\langle p_P\rangle<0$; the prescribed medium is active over a cycle and returns energy to the electromagnetic field. Thus positivity cannot be asserted without a passivity assumption.

ED:176.title: Maxwell stress gives the pressure on a conducting surface
ED:176.objective: Derive the vacuum Maxwell stress tensor from local momentum balance, evaluate its traction on a conducting surface, and determine the net direction when electric and magnetic pressures compete.
ED:176.statement:
A stationary planar conductor occupies $z<0$ and vacuum occupies $z>0$. Let the unit normal pointing outward from the conductor into vacuum be $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Immediately outside the conductor,
$$\mathbf E=E_n\hat{\mathbf n},\qquad \mathbf B=\mathbf B_t,\qquad \mathbf B_t\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0,$$
where $B_t=|\mathbf B_t|$. Assume the fields immediately inside are negligible, so the requested force is due to the one-sided exterior fields. Use SI units and the vacuum Maxwell equations.

(a) Starting from the vacuum Lorentz force density $\mathbf f=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B$, derive the momentum balance
$$\mathbf f=\nabla\cdot\mathbf T-\partial_t\mathbf g$$
by finding the Maxwell stress tensor $\mathbf T$ and field momentum density $\mathbf g$.

(b) Use a vanishingly thin pillbox to show that the electromagnetic force per unit area on the conductor is $\mathbf t=\mathbf T_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$. Evaluate this traction for the stated one-sided fields, identifying the electric outward pressure and magnetic inward pressure.

(c) Take $E_n=6.00\times10^7\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $B_t=0.180\ \mathrm T$. Using $\epsilon_0=8.8541878128\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$ and $\mu_0=1.25663706212\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{H/m}$, calculate both pressures and the net traction, including its direction.

(d) Check the result independently using the induced surface charge and surface current, with the force evaluated using the average of the fields on the two sides. Also state the equality condition at which the net normal pressure vanishes.

abla\cdot(\mathbf a\mathbf a-	frac12a^2\mathbf I)=\mathbf a(
abla\cdot\mathbf a)-\mathbf a	imes(
abla	imes\mathbf a)$ may be used.
The Maxwell stress tensor itself may not be quoted without derivation.

Once the stress tensor is obtained, apply it directly to the declared outward normal. For the independent check, infer the surface sources from field jumps and use half of each discontinuous exterior field as the field acting on its own surface source.

Correctly computes $15.94\ \mathrm{kPa}$ electric, $12.89\ \mathrm{kPa}$ magnetic, and $3.05\ \mathrm{kPa}$ net outward, with a valid surface-source or equality-condition check.

The remaining time-dependent terms combine through $\partial_t(\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)$.
When calculating $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$, use $\mathbf E\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=E_n$ but $\mathbf B_t\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0$; this difference determines the opposite pressure signs.

ED:176.canonicalSolution:
In vacuum,
$$\rho=\epsilon_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf E,\qquad \mathbf J=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\nabla\times\mathbf B-\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E.$$
The dyadic identity and Faraday's law give
$$\nabla\cdot\left[\epsilon_0\left(\mathbf E\mathbf E-\frac12E^2\mathbf I\right)\right]
=\rho\mathbf E-\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times(\nabla\times\mathbf E)
=\rho\mathbf E+\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Because $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$,
$$\nabla\cdot\left[\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\mathbf B\mathbf B-\frac12B^2\mathbf I\right)\right]
=\frac{1}{\mu_0}(\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B.$$
Ampere-Maxwell's law then gives
$$\frac{1}{\mu_0}(\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B
=\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0(\partial_t\mathbf E)\times\mathbf B.$$
Adding the two equations produces
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0\partial_t(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B).$$
Consequently,
$$\boxed{\mathbf f=\nabla\cdot\mathbf T-\partial_t\mathbf g,}$$
with
$$\boxed{\mathbf T=\epsilon_0\left(\mathbf E\mathbf E-\frac12E^2\mathbf I\right)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\mathbf B\mathbf B-\frac12B^2\mathbf I\right),}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B.}$$
Both parts of $\mathbf T$ have units of pressure: $\epsilon_0E^2$ and $B^2/\mu_0$ are in $\mathrm{N/m^2}$.

Integrate the momentum balance over a thin pillbox containing the interface. As its thickness tends to zero, the finite field-momentum term vanishes with the volume. The inner-face stress is zero by assumption, while the exterior face has outward pillbox normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$. Thus the force per unit area on the conductor is
$$\mathbf t=\mathbf T_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
For the normal electric field,
$$\left(\mathbf E\mathbf E-\frac12E^2\mathbf I\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}
=\frac12E_n^2\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
For the tangential magnetic field, $\mathbf B_t\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0$, so
$$\left(\mathbf B_t\mathbf B_t-\frac12B_t^2\mathbf I\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}
=-\frac12B_t^2\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\mathbf t=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E_n^2}{2}-\frac{B_t^2}{2\mu_0}\right)\hat{\mathbf n}.}$$
The electric pressure
$$\boxed{p_E=\frac{\epsilon_0E_n^2}{2}}$$
is outward, toward the vacuum. The magnetic pressure
$$\boxed{p_B=\frac{B_t^2}{2\mu_0}}$$
is inward, into the conductor.

Numerically,
$$p_E=\frac{(8.8541878128\times10^{-12})(6.00\times10^7)^2}{2}
=1.59375\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}=15.94\ \mathrm{kPa},$$
while
$$p_B=\frac{(0.180)^2}{2(1.25663706212\times10^{-6})}
=1.28916\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}=12.89\ \mathrm{kPa}.$$
Hence
$$\boxed{\mathbf t=(3.05\times10^3\ \mathrm{Pa})\hat{\mathbf n}.}$$
The net pressure is $3.05\ \mathrm{kPa}$ outward from the conductor into the vacuum.

For an independent surface-source check, the electric boundary condition gives
$$\sigma=\epsilon_0E_n.$$
The electric field acting on the surface charge excludes its singular self-field and equals the average of the two limiting fields, $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{avg}}=E_n\hat{\mathbf n}/2$. Therefore
$$\frac{\mathbf F_E}{A}=\sigma\mathbf E_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\epsilon_0E_n^2}{2}\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
The magnetic boundary condition gives the surface current
$$\mathbf K=\hat{\mathbf n}\times\frac{\mathbf B_t}{\mu_0}.$$
Using $\mathbf B_{\mathrm{avg}}=\mathbf B_t/2$,
$$\frac{\mathbf F_B}{A}=\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{avg}}
=\frac{(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf B_t)\times\mathbf B_t}{2\mu_0}
=-\frac{B_t^2}{2\mu_0}\hat{\mathbf n},$$
which independently confirms both signs and factors of one-half.

The net pressure vanishes when
$$\epsilon_0E_n^2=\frac{B_t^2}{\mu_0},$$
or
$$\boxed{|E_n|=cB_t,\qquad c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}.}$$
For the numerical fields, $cB_t\approx5.40\times10^7\ \mathrm{V/m}<|E_n|$, consistently predicting an outward net traction. If nonzero fields existed inside the conductor, the required traction would instead be the stress jump $(\mathbf T_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf T_{\mathrm{in}})\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$.

ED:177.title: Stress and energy agree on the force pulling a dielectric wedge
ED:177.objective: Derive the fixed-voltage insertion force on a dielectric wedge by an energy ledger that includes battery work, reproduce it with macroscopic Maxwell stress, and verify the agreement numerically and dimensionally.
ED:177.statement:
Two long, perfectly conducting parallel plates occupy $0<x<L$, $0<y<w$, at $z=0$ and $z=d$. The lower plate is maintained at potential $V$ and the upper plate at zero, so the principal field points along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. A rigid linear, homogeneous, isotropic dielectric wedge has relative permittivity $\epsilon_r$ and fills the entire gap over the footprint $0<x'<x$, $0<y<w$; its active portion has constant width $w$, while any remote taper lies outside the capacitor. Vacuum fills the remaining footprint. The wedge is translated quasistatically in the $+\hat{\mathbf x}$ direction by increasing $x$. Assume $d\ll w,L$, that the dielectric nose and both plate ends are separated by several gap widths, and that electrostriction, gravity, friction, and position-dependent external fringe capacitance are negligible. Local fringing near the dielectric nose may transmit force but must lie inside the stress control surface. The voltage is held fixed by an ideal battery. This is electrostatics, so no phasor convention is used.

(a) Derive $C(x)$ directly from the plate charge. Use a battery-field-mechanical energy ledger to show why the force is $+d(CV^2/2)/dx$, rather than the negative derivative of the stored field energy at fixed voltage.

(b) Enclose the dielectric nose with a rectangular control surface. Its rear face lies in the uniform dielectric region with outward normal $-\hat{\mathbf x}$, and its front face lies in the uniform vacuum region with outward normal $+\hat{\mathbf x}$. Evaluate the $x$-directed Maxwell-stress traction on these faces and show that it gives the same force. Explain why the other faces do not contribute to the lateral force under the stated approximation.

(c) For $L=0.400\,\mathrm{m}$, $x=0.150\,\mathrm{m}$, $w=0.0800\,\mathrm{m}$, $d=2.00\,\mathrm{mm}$, $\epsilon_r=4.20$, and $V=500\,\mathrm{V}$, calculate the force. Independently check it using the energy-density difference, audit its SI dimensions, and state two limiting checks.
permittedResults: In a linear isotropic dielectric, $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ with $\epsilon=\epsilon_r\epsilon_0$, and the electrostatic energy density is $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$.

For quasistatic charge $dQ$ delivered by an ideal source at voltage $V$, the source supplies energy $V\,dQ$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat the dielectric-filled and vacuum-filled footprints as parallel regions sharing the same plate voltage. First derive their free plate charges and hence $C(x)$. At fixed voltage, distinguish battery work from the change in field energy. For the independent stress calculation, place the control faces in uniform regions so that only the difference between dielectric and vacuum normal stresses remains.

commonErrors.description: Treating the fixed-voltage capacitor as an isolated system and writing $F_x=-d(CV^2/2)/dx$ without including the battery energy $V\,dQ$.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted force has the wrong sign and incorrectly says the dielectric is expelled.

commonErrors.description: Using the dielectric stress or energy density alone instead of subtracting the vacuum traction on the opposite control face.
commonErrors.consequence: The result remains nonzero when $\epsilon_r=1$ and overestimates the physical insertion force.

hintTree.content: Both side-by-side regions have field magnitude $V/d$. Integrate $\mathbf D\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}$ over the lower plate separately over areas $wx$ and $w(L-x)$.

The leading parallel-plate field is
$$\mathbf E=\frac{V}{d}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
The dielectric and vacuum regions share this voltage because both touch the same conducting plates. The free charge on the lower plate is therefore
$$Q(x)=\int \mathbf D\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}\,dA
=\epsilon\frac{V}{d}wx+\epsilon_0\frac{V}{d}w(L-x).$$
Thus
$$C(x)=\frac{Q}{V}=\frac{w}{d}\left[\epsilon_0L+(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)x\right],$$
so
$$\frac{dC}{dx}=\frac{w}{d}(\epsilon-\epsilon_0).$$

The field energy follows by integrating $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$ over both volumes:
$$U_{\mathrm f}=\frac12\epsilon E^2wxd+\frac12\epsilon_0E^2w(L-x)d
=\frac12C(x)V^2.$$
At fixed $V$, an increment $dC$ requires $dQ=V\,dC$. The battery supplies
$$dW_{\mathrm b}=V\,dQ=V^2dC,$$
while the field-energy increase is
$$dU_{\mathrm f}=\frac12V^2dC.$$
Energy conservation in the quasistatic process gives $dW_{\mathrm b}=dU_{\mathrm f}+dW_{\mathrm{mech}}$, where $dW_{\mathrm{mech}}$ is work done by the electric field on the wedge. Hence
$$dW_{\mathrm{mech}}=\frac12V^2dC,$$
and the insertion force is
$$F_x=\frac{dW_{\mathrm{mech}}}{dx}=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac12CV^2\right)
=\frac12(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\frac{w}{d}V^2>0.$$
Equivalently, the fixed-voltage mechanical potential is $U_{\mathrm f}-VQ=-CV^2/2$, whose negative derivative gives the same positive force.

For the stress calculation, define
$$u_{\mathrm d}=\frac12\epsilon E^2,\qquad u_0=\frac12\epsilon_0E^2.$$
Because $E_x=0$, the normal stress on a face perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is $T_{xx}=-u$. On the rear dielectric face, whose outward normal is $-\hat{\mathbf x}$, the $x$ traction is
$$\left(\mathbf T_{\mathrm d}\cdot(-\hat{\mathbf x})\right)_x=+u_{\mathrm d}.$$
On the front vacuum face, whose outward normal is $+\hat{\mathbf x}$, it is
$$\left(\mathbf T_0\cdot\hat{\mathbf x}\right)_x=-u_0.$$
Each face has area $wd$, so the net stress force is
$$F_x=(u_{\mathrm d}-u_0)wd
=\frac12(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\left(\frac{V}{d}\right)^2wd
=\frac12(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\frac{w}{d}V^2.$$
This agrees with the energy result. The faces normal to $\hat{\mathbf y}$ have no $x$ traction in the uniform approximation. On surfaces immediately adjacent to ideal conductors, the tangential component $E_x$ vanishes, so $T_{xz}=E_xD_z=0$. The localized nose fringe field is enclosed rather than discarded; placing the front and rear faces in uniform regions makes its integrated effect equal to the stress difference above.

Numerically,
$$\frac{dC}{dx}=\epsilon_0(\epsilon_r-1)\frac{w}{d}
=(8.85419\times10^{-12})(3.20)\frac{0.0800}{0.00200}
=1.13334\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F/m}.$$
Therefore
$$F_x=\frac12(500)^2(1.13334\times10^{-9})
=1.42\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N,$$
directed into the capacitor. Independently, $E=2.50\times10^5\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and
$$u_{\mathrm d}-u_0=\frac12\epsilon_0(3.20)E^2=0.885\,\mathrm{J/m^3}.$$
Multiplication by $wd=(0.0800)(0.00200)=1.60\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ gives $1.42\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N$. Dimensionally, $V^2(dC/dx)$ has units $\mathrm{V^2F/m}=\mathrm{J/m}=\mathrm N$. The force vanishes when $\epsilon_r\to1$ or $V\to0$, and it is unchanged when the voltage polarity is reversed.

ED:178.title: An anisotropic polarizable body feels torque without net force
ED:178.objective: Construct the induced-dipole energy of an anisotropic body, including the one-half factor, and use it to calculate torque, equilibrium orientations, and translational force in a uniform electric field.
ED:178.statement:
A small neutral body is confined to rotate in the $xy$ plane. Its orthonormal body axes are $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$, with $\hat{\mathbf e}_1\times\hat{\mathbf e}_2=\hat{\mathbf z}$. It has no permanent dipole and has the linear polarizability tensor
$$\boldsymbol\alpha=\alpha_1\hat{\mathbf e}_1\hat{\mathbf e}_1+\alpha_2\hat{\mathbf e}_2\hat{\mathbf e}_2,$$
where $\alpha_1,\alpha_2>0$. An ideal fixed source produces a static, spatially uniform field
$$\mathbf E=E(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf e}_1+\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf e}_2),$$
where positive $\theta$ is measured from $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$. If the body's laboratory orientation is $\phi$ and the fixed field direction is $\beta$, then $\theta=\beta-\phi$. Treat the body in the electric-dipole approximation, neglect field gradients, higher multipoles, saturation, and interactions with boundaries. No phasors are used.

(a) Model the reversible internal polarization energy along each principal axis and minimize over the induced dipole components. Derive the equilibrium induced dipole and its field-dependent energy, explicitly establishing the factor $1/2$.

(b) Derive the $z$-directed torque on the body, identify all stable and unstable orientations for $\alpha_1>\alpha_2$, and state how the classification changes for $\alpha_2>\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$.

(c) Show from the energy that the net translational force is zero even though the torque can be nonzero. Check the torque independently with $\mathbf p\times\mathbf E$.

(d) For $\alpha_1=6.00\times10^{-29}\,\mathrm{C\,m^2/V}$, $\alpha_2=2.00\times10^{-29}\,\mathrm{C\,m^2/V}$, $E=3.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{V/m}$, and $\theta=30.0^\circ$, calculate the torque, give its direction, and audit its SI dimensions.
permittedResults: The interaction energy of a specified dipole in an external electrostatic field is $-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf E$.
For a generalized orientation coordinate $\phi$, the torque is $\tau_z=-\partial U/\partial\phi$ at fixed external sources.
The torque on a localized electric dipole can be checked using $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf p\times\mathbf E$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Introduce the induced dipole components as variables rather than immediately substituting $\mathbf p=\boldsymbol\alpha\mathbf E$. Add quadratic internal deformation energy to the dipole-field interaction and minimize. Then differentiate the minimized energy with respect to the body angle $\phi$, remembering that $\theta=\beta-\phi$, and separately differentiate with respect to position to test for force.

milestones.criterion: Constructs and minimizes the quadratic internal-plus-interaction energy, obtaining $p_i=\alpha_iE_i$ and $U=-\mathbf E\cdot\boldsymbol\alpha\mathbf E/2$ with a valid explanation of the one-half factor.
Uses $\theta=\beta-\phi$ to obtain the correctly signed torque and correctly classifies equilibria for both anisotropy orderings and the isotropic limit.
Shows that spatial uniformity gives zero net force, confirms the torque with $\mathbf p\times\mathbf E$, and obtains $1.56\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{N\,m}$ along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ with correct units.

commonErrors.description: Substituting the induced dipole into $-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf E$ and taking that expression as the total energy, thereby omitting the internal polarization energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The orientational energy and torque are too large by a factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Using $\tau_z=-dU/d\theta$ even though $\theta$ is the field angle relative to the body and satisfies $d\theta/d\phi=-1$.
commonErrors.consequence: The torque direction is reversed and would rotate the more polarizable axis away from a stable alignment.

hintTree.content: For principal component $p_i$, linear response is generated by an internal energy whose derivative with respect to $p_i$ is $p_i/\alpha_i$. Add the interaction term $-p_iE_i$ before minimizing.
After minimization, substitute $E_1=E\cos\theta$ and $E_2=E\sin\theta$. The torque on the body is not $-dU/d\theta$ because increasing the body angle decreases $\theta$.
For the independent check, compute $(\mathbf p\times\mathbf E)_z=p_1E_2-p_2E_1$. For translation, ask whether the minimized energy contains the body's position.

ED:178.canonicalSolution:
Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be the induced dipole components. Linear restoring response along axis $i$ is represented by the internal energy $p_i^2/(2\alpha_i)$, since its derivative is $p_i/\alpha_i$. Including the dipole-field interaction gives
$$U(p_1,p_2)=\frac{p_1^2}{2\alpha_1}+\frac{p_2^2}{2\alpha_2}-p_1E_1-p_2E_2.$$
Equilibrium requires
$$\frac{\partial U}{\partial p_i}=\frac{p_i}{\alpha_i}-E_i=0,$$
so
$$p_i=\alpha_iE_i,$$
or
$$\mathbf p=\alpha_1E\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf e}_1+\alpha_2E\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf e}_2.$$
Substitution into the full internal-plus-interaction energy gives, for each component, $p_i^2/(2\alpha_i)-p_iE_i=-\alpha_iE_i^2/2$. Therefore the minimized orientational energy is
$$U(\theta)=-\frac12\mathbf E\cdot\boldsymbol\alpha\mathbf E
=-\frac12E^2\left(\alpha_1\cos^2\theta+\alpha_2\sin^2\theta\right).$$
The factor $1/2$ arises because part of the interaction work is stored as reversible internal polarization energy; replacing the induced dipole directly in $-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf E$ would count the field-dependent interaction twice.

Because $\theta=\beta-\phi$, one has $\partial\theta/\partial\phi=-1$. Thus the torque on the body is
$$\tau_z=-\frac{\partial U}{\partial\phi}=\frac{\partial U}{\partial\theta}
=(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)E^2\sin\theta\cos\theta
=\frac12(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)E^2\sin2\theta.$$
For $\alpha_1>\alpha_2$, the energy is lowest when the more polarizable axis $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is parallel or antiparallel to the field: $\theta=0$ and $\pi$ are stable. The orientations $\theta=\pi/2$ and $3\pi/2$ are unstable. This follows directly from
$$\frac{d^2U}{d\theta^2}=(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)E^2\cos2\theta.$$
If $\alpha_2>\alpha_1$, the stability classifications interchange, so $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ aligns with the field. If $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$, $U$ is independent of $\theta$ and every orientation is neutrally stable with zero torque.

The field and polarizabilities are spatially uniform, so the minimized energy contains no center-of-mass coordinate $\mathbf r$. Hence
$$\mathbf F=-\boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf r}U=\mathbf 0.$$
The torque can nevertheless be nonzero because $U$ depends on orientation. Independently,
$$\left(\mathbf p\times\mathbf E\right)_z=p_1E_2-p_2E_1
=(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)E^2\sin\theta\cos\theta,$$
which agrees with the energy derivative and its sign.

For the supplied values,
$$\tau_z=\frac12(6.00-2.00)\times10^{-29}(3.00\times10^5)^2\sin60.0^\circ.$$
Therefore
$$\tau_z=1.56\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{N\,m}.$$
It points along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, rotating $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward the field and reducing $\theta$. The dimensional check is
$$[\alpha E^2]=\frac{\mathrm{C\,m^2}}{\mathrm V}\frac{\mathrm{V^2}}{\mathrm{m^2}}=\mathrm{C\,V}=\mathrm J=\mathrm{N\,m}.$$
As a component check, $p_1=1.56\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$ and $p_2=3.00\times10^{-24}\,\mathrm{C\,m}$; evaluating $p_1E_2-p_2E_1$ reproduces $1.56\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{N\,m}$.

ED:179.title: Field momentum closes the Lorentz-force balance
ED:179.objective: Derive the local electromagnetic linear-momentum balance directly from Maxwell's equations, distinguish the momentum-flux tensor from the conventional Maxwell stress tensor, and interpret nonzero surface tractions in a uniform crossed-field control volume.
ED:179.statement:
Work in SI units with real time-domain fields; no phasors are used. Vacuum has $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E$, $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0$, and $c^{-2}=\epsilon_0\mu_0$. Sources $\rho(\mathbf r,t)$ and $\mathbf J(\mathbf r,t)$ may be present, and all fields are differentiable in the region considered.

Define the field momentum density $\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$. Use the momentum-flux sign convention
$$T_{ij}=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\right)\delta_{ij}-\epsilon_0E_iE_j-\frac{1}{\mu_0}B_iB_j,$$
so that $\mathbf T=-\boldsymbol\sigma$, where $\boldsymbol\sigma$ is the conventional Maxwell stress tensor. For a surface whose unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ points outward from a field control volume, $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$ is outward field-momentum flux per area; the conventional stress traction is $\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=-\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$.

(a) Starting only from Maxwell's equations, derive
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=-\left(\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B\right).$$
State its integral form for a fixed volume $V$ with outward normal.

(b) Let a rectangular control volume of side lengths $L_x,L_y,L_z$ lie wholly inside a broad region with stationary uniform fields $\mathbf E=E_0\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf y}$, where $(\hat{\mathbf x},\hat{\mathbf y},\hat{\mathbf z})$ is right-handed. Calculate $\mathbf g$, all three independent diagonal entries of $\mathbf T$, and $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$ on each pair of faces. Verify the balance by summing boundary fluxes, rather than by merely observing that $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=0$. Interpret the nonzero individual tractions and include a dimensional and limiting check.

so the tensor in the problem is $T_{ij}=-\sigma_{ij}$.

$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_E=\epsilon_0\left[(\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E)\mathbf E+(\mathbf E\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla)\mathbf E-\frac12\boldsymbol\nabla E^2\right].$$
Using
$$(\mathbf E\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla)\mathbf E-\frac12\boldsymbol\nabla E^2=-\mathbf E\times(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf E),$$
and Maxwell's equations,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_E=\rho\mathbf E-\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf E)=\rho\mathbf E+\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
For the magnetic part, $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ gives
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_B=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[(\mathbf B\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla)\mathbf B-\frac12\boldsymbol\nabla B^2\right]=\frac{1}{\mu_0}(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B.$$

$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_B=\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0(\partial_t\mathbf E)\times\mathbf B.$$
Adding the two parts and applying the time-product rule,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0\partial_t(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B).$$
Since $\mathbf T=-\boldsymbol\sigma$ and $\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$,
$$\boxed{\partial_t\mathbf g+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=-\mathbf f_L},\qquad \mathbf f_L=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B.$$
For a fixed volume,
$$\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\int_V\mathbf g\,dV+\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA=-\int_V\mathbf f_L\,dV}.$$
Equivalently, the force on matter in $V$ is $\int_V\mathbf f_LdV=\oint_{\partial V}\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA-d\int_V\mathbf g\,dV/dt$.

For the crossed fields,
$$\mathbf g=\epsilon_0E_0B_0\,\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Let $u_E=\epsilon_0E_0^2/2$ and $u_B=B_0^2/(2\mu_0)$. In the ordered basis $(\hat{\mathbf x},\hat{\mathbf y},\hat{\mathbf z})$,
$$\mathbf T=\begin{pmatrix}u_B-u_E&0&0\\0&u_E-u_B&0\\0&0&u_E+u_B\end{pmatrix}.$$
Consequently,
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm\hat{\mathbf x}:&\quad \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm(u_B-u_E)\hat{\mathbf x},\\
\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm\hat{\mathbf y}:&\quad \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm(u_E-u_B)\hat{\mathbf y},\\
\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm\hat{\mathbf z}:&\quad \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm(u_E+u_B)\hat{\mathbf z}.
\end{aligned}$$
The two faces in each pair have equal area and opposite flux, so
$$\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA=\mathbf0.$$
The fields are stationary, so $d\int_V\mathbf g\,dV/dt=0$, and the integral balance gives zero net bulk Lorentz force. Nevertheless, each cut carries a generally nonzero traction; cancellation occurs only after all oriented faces are included. The conventional stress traction on the same oriented cut is the negative of the listed momentum flux.

Both $u_E$ and $u_B$ have units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, while $[\mathbf g]=\mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-3}}$. Thus $\partial_t\mathbf g$ and $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T$ both have units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. As a limiting check, if $B_0=0$, then $T_{xx}=-u_E$ and $T_{yy}=T_{zz}=u_E$, corresponding to the opposite-sign conventional electric tension along $\mathbf E$ and transverse pressure, with paired face fluxes still canceling.

ED:180.title: Angular momentum balance requires a symmetric stress tensor
ED:180.objective: Convert local linear-momentum conservation into local angular-momentum conservation, identify precisely where stress-tensor symmetry is required, and track field and mechanical angular momentum during the quasistatic establishment of crossed coaxial fields.
ED:180.statement:
Use right-handed cylindrical coordinates $(r,\phi,z)$ with $\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Work in SI vacuum, $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0$, with real time-domain fields and no phasors. Adopt the momentum balance and flux convention
$$\partial_t g_i+\partial_jT_{ij}=-f_i,$$
where $\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$, $\mathbf f=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B$, and
$$T_{ij}=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\right)\delta_{ij}-\epsilon_0E_iE_j-\frac{1}{\mu_0}B_iB_j.$$

(a) Define $\boldsymbol\ell=\mathbf r\times\mathbf g$ and $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf f$. By an index calculation, derive the local angular-momentum balance and its flux tensor. Exhibit the extra term that would survive for a nonsymmetric momentum-flux tensor, and explain why it vanishes here.

(b) Two very long, thin, electrically insulating coaxial cylindrical shells have radii $a<b$ and fixed charge per unit length $+\lambda$ and $-\lambda$, respectively. End effects are neglected. In the annulus $a<r<b$, an externally produced final magnetic field is $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Derive the radial electric field, then calculate the electromagnetic angular momentum per unit axial length and determine its direction for $\lambda>0$ and $B_0>0$.

(c) To check the boundary torque signs, suppose the magnetic field is raised slowly from zero as $\mathbf B=B(t)\hat{\mathbf z}$, approximately uniform over every disk $r<b$. Neglect radiation and fringing, but retain the Faraday-induced azimuthal electric field. The outward normals of the annular field volume are $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $r=b$ and $-\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $r=a$. Derive $E_\phi(r,t)$, find the torque per unit length on each charged shell, and show that their sum is opposite to the rate of change of field angular momentum. Reproduce the same sign ledger from the radial angular-momentum flux. State what happens to the boundary torques after the ramp ends and give a dimensional or limiting check.
permittedResults: The local linear-momentum balance $\partial_tg_i+\partial_jT_{ij}=-f_i$ with the stated momentum-flux convention
The Levi-Civita representation $(\mathbf A\times\mathbf B)_i=\epsilon_{ikl}A_kB_l$ and the spatial product rule
Gauss's law, Maxwell-Faraday's law, and cylindrical symmetry

acceptableStrategies.description: Multiply each component of the linear-momentum balance by $\epsilon_{ikl}x_k$ and apply the product rule before identifying the angular flux. For the coaxial application, compute the azimuthal field momentum and integrate $\ell_z=rg_\phi$ over the annular cross-section. During the magnetic ramp, use Faraday's law to calculate both direct shell torques and the off-diagonal flux component $T_{\phi r}$.

milestones.criterion: Derives the angular-momentum flux tensor by a correct product-rule calculation, displays the antisymmetric-stress term, and explains why symmetry of the Maxwell tensor removes it.
Derives the coaxial electric field and obtains the correct magnitude and $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ direction of the stored angular momentum per unit length.

Calculates both Faraday-induced shell torques with the correct inner and outer signs, matches their sum to the field angular-momentum rate and radial flux, and supplies a valid static or limiting check.

commonErrors.description: Treats the position factor $x_k$ as constant when taking $\partial_j(\epsilon_{ikl}x_kT_{lj})$.
commonErrors.consequence: The antisymmetric-stress term is lost, so angular-momentum conservation is asserted without establishing the required symmetry of $T_{ij}$.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=+\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ or assigns $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ as the annulus's inner outward normal.
commonErrors.consequence: The stored angular momentum or one boundary-torque contribution receives the wrong sign, preventing the shell and field angular-momentum ledgers from closing.

hintTree.content: When differentiating $\epsilon_{ikl}x_kT_{lj}$ with respect to $x_j$, do not treat $x_k$ as constant. The derivative of the position factor produces a contraction of $T_{lj}$ with the antisymmetric Levi-Civita symbol.
In the annulus, cylindrical Gauss surfaces give $E_r\propto1/r$. Since $\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=-\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$, the relevant axial angular-momentum density is $\ell_z=rg_\phi$.

During the ramp, apply Faraday's law to a circle of radius $R<b$. For the flux check, only $T_{\phi r}$ contributes to axial angular momentum crossing a cylindrical surface, and the inner surface carries the outward normal $-\hat{\mathbf r}$.

ED:180.canonicalSolution:
Write
$$\ell_i=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kg_l,\qquad \tau_i=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kf_l.$$
Multiplying the linear-momentum equation for component $l$ by $\epsilon_{ikl}x_k$ gives
$$\partial_t\ell_i+\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\partial_jT_{lj}=-\tau_i.$$
Define the angular-momentum flux tensor
$$M_{ij}=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kT_{lj}.$$
Its divergence is
$$\partial_jM_{ij}=\epsilon_{ikl}\delta_{jk}T_{lj}+\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\partial_jT_{lj}=\epsilon_{ijl}T_{lj}+\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\partial_jT_{lj}.$$
Therefore the general balance is
$$\partial_t\ell_i+\partial_jM_{ij}=-\tau_i+\epsilon_{ijl}T_{lj}.$$
The contraction $\epsilon_{ijl}T_{lj}$ selects the antisymmetric part of $T_{lj}$. The stated electromagnetic tensor is symmetric because $\delta_{ij}$, $E_iE_j$, and $B_iB_j$ are all symmetric. Hence
$$\boxed{\partial_t\ell_i+\partial_jM_{ij}=-\tau_i},\qquad \boxed{M_{ij}=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kT_{lj}}.$$
Thus local orbital angular momentum follows from linear-momentum conservation only after the internal stress contribution is shown to be symmetric.

For the coaxial shells, a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $L$, with $a<r<b$, encloses charge $\lambda L$. Gauss's law gives
$$E_r(2\pi rL)=\frac{\lambda L}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \mathbf E=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0r}\hat{\mathbf r}.$$
The field momentum density is
$$\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B=-\epsilon_0E_rB_0\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2\pi r}\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}.$$
The axial component of angular-momentum density is
$$\ell_z=rg_\phi=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2\pi}.$$
Integrating over the annular cross-section gives
$$\frac{L_{\mathrm{field},z}}{L}=\int_a^b\ell_z(2\pi r\,dr)=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2}(b^2-a^2).$$
Thus
$$\boxed{\frac{\mathbf L_{\mathrm{field}}}{L}=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2}(b^2-a^2)\hat{\mathbf z}}.$$
For $\lambda>0$ and $B_0>0$, the stored field angular momentum points along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$.

During the slow ramp, Maxwell-Faraday's law on a circle of radius $R<b$, oriented with normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, gives
$$2\pi R E_\phi(R,t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\left(\pi R^2B\right),$$
so
$$E_\phi(R,t)=-\frac{R}{2}\dot B(t).$$
A shell carrying charge per length $q'$ experiences tangential force per length $q'E_\phi$ and axial torque per length $Rq'E_\phi$. Hence
$$\frac{\tau_{a,z}}{L}=\lambda aE_\phi(a)=-\frac{\lambda a^2}{2}\dot B,$$
while the outer shell carries $q'=-\lambda$ and therefore
$$\frac{\tau_{b,z}}{L}=(-\lambda)bE_\phi(b)=+\frac{\lambda b^2}{2}\dot B.$$
For $\lambda>0$ and $\dot B>0$, the inner shell torque points along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, the outer torque points along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, and the larger outer moment arm makes the net torque positive:
$$\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{shells},z}}{L}=\frac{\lambda}{2}(b^2-a^2)\dot B.$$
Meanwhile,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{L_{\mathrm{field},z}}{L}\right)=-\frac{\lambda}{2}(b^2-a^2)\dot B,$$
so
$$\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{L_{\mathrm{field},z}}{L}\right)+\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{shells},z}}{L}=0}.$$

The same result follows from angular-momentum flux. During the ramp, the relevant off-diagonal component is
$$T_{\phi r}=-\epsilon_0E_\phi E_r=-\frac{\lambda E_\phi}{2\pi r}.$$
The radial flux density of axial angular momentum is $M_{zr}=rT_{\phi r}$. Per unit axial length, the outer and inner surface contributions are respectively
$$2\pi b\,[bT_{\phi r}(b)]=-\lambda bE_\phi(b)=\frac{\tau_{b,z}}{L},$$
$$2\pi a\,[-aT_{\phi r}(a)]=\lambda aE_\phi(a)=\frac{\tau_{a,z}}{L},$$
where the minus sign in the second expression comes from the annulus's inner outward normal $-\hat{\mathbf r}$. Their sum is the positive outward angular-momentum flux, and the vacuum balance in the annulus reads $d(L_{\mathrm{field},z}/L)/dt+$ outward flux $=0$.

After the ramp, $\dot B=0$, so $E_\phi=0$, $T_{\phi r}=0$, and both boundary torques vanish even though the static crossed fields retain nonzero angular momentum. Dimensionally, $[\lambda B_0(b^2-a^2)]=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, which is angular momentum per unit length. The result vanishes as $b\to a$ and reverses direction if either $\lambda$ or $B_0$ changes sign.

ED:181.objective: Derive the electromagnetic fields from scalar and vector potentials, determine the time-dependent scalar-potential transformation required by a gauge change, and verify field invariance in a dimensionally consistent construction.
ED:181.statement:
Work in right-handed Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ over a time interval $I$. All fields and potentials are sufficiently smooth for spatial and temporal derivatives to commute. Use real-time SI quantities, not phasors. Assume vacuum constitutive relations $\mathbf{D}=\epsilon_0\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{B}/\mu_0$, although no constitutive relation is needed below; make no approximation. (a) Starting from the homogeneous Maxwell equations, derive representations $\mathbf{B}=
abla	imes\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{E}=-
abla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf{A}$. (b) Under $\mathbf{A}'=\mathbf{A}+
abla\chi$, derive the most general transformation of $\phi$ that preserves $\mathbf{E}$, including any spatially constant freedom. Fix the same scalar-potential reference to obtain $\phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi$, and verify both fields exactly. (c) Take constants $E_0$ and $B_0$ and the initial potentials $\phi=-E_0x$ and $\mathbf{A}=B_0x\,\hat{\mathbf y}$. The identities $

acceptableStrategies.description: First use the two homogeneous Maxwell equations to introduce the potentials. Compare the primed and unprimed electric fields after changing $\mathbf{A}$; requiring their difference to vanish determines the sign of the scalar transformation up to a function of time. In the concrete construction, evaluate the gradient and time derivative of $\chi$ componentwise so that both cancellations remain visible.

milestones.criterion: Correctly derives both potential representations from the homogeneous Maxwell equations on the stated contractible domain.
Obtains $\phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi+C(t)$ and verifies the separate gradient and time-derivative cancellations in both fields.
Computes the concrete primed potentials and fields with the two curl terms, correct SI dimensions, and the $\lambda\to0$ check.

commonErrors.description: Using $\phi'=\phi+\partial_t\chi$ instead of the required minus sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The gauge contributions to the electric field add rather than cancel, producing $\mathbf{E}'=\mathbf{E}-2\nabla\partial_t\chi$.

commonErrors.description: Computing $B'_z$ from $\partial_xA'_y$ alone and omitting $-\partial_yA'_x$.
commonErrors.consequence: This gives the spurious result $B'_z=B_0+\lambda t$ and falsely suggests that the gauge transformation changes the magnetic field.

hintTree.content: After writing $\mathbf{B}$ as a curl, substitute it into Faraday's law and identify a curl-free vector field.
Set $\mathbf{E}'-\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{0}$ and collect the scalar terms inside one spatial gradient; a zero gradient permits a function of time.
For $\chi=\lambda txy$, compute $\nabla\chi$ and $\partial_t\nabla\chi$ separately, and retain both terms in the $z$ component of the curl.

ED:181.canonicalSolution:
The homogeneous magnetic equation gives
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0.$$
Because $\mathbb{R}^3$ is contractible, a smooth vector potential exists such that
$$\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}.$$
Faraday's law then becomes
$$\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\partial_t(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}),$$
so commuting the derivatives gives
$$\nabla\times(\mathbf{E}+\partial_t\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{0}.$$
The quantity in parentheses is therefore a gradient. Defining its negative potential by $\mathbf{E}+\partial_t\mathbf{A}=-\nabla\phi$ yields
$$\mathbf{E}=-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf{A}.$$
Now let $\mathbf{A}'=\mathbf{A}+\nabla\chi$. The magnetic field is unchanged because
$$\mathbf{B}'=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}'=\mathbf{B}+\nabla\times\nabla\chi=\mathbf{B}.$$
For the electric field,

ED:182.title: Coulomb gauge leaves a residual harmonic freedom
ED:182.objective: Derive the residual gauge equation in Coulomb gauge, prove how boundary data eliminate that freedom, and construct a nonconstant harmonic gauge transformation showing that topology alone is insufficient.
ED:182.statement: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be a bounded, connected, simply connected region with sufficiently smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$ and outward unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$. Use right-handed Cartesian coordinates, real-time SI fields, and smooth potentials. Assume vacuum constitutive relations, although the argument is purely kinematic and allows arbitrary sources in $\Omega$. No phasors or approximations are used. At each time impose Coulomb gauge, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A}=0$. (a) For $\mathbf{A}'=\mathbf{A}+\nabla\chi$ and $\phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi$, derive the differential equation obeyed by every residual gauge function that preserves Coulomb gauge. (b) Use Green's first identity to show that homogeneous Dirichlet data $\chi|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ eliminate the residual freedom. Explain what homogeneous Neumann data $\partial_n\chi=0$ leave and what additional normalization removes it. (c) When boundary values are not fixed, construct a nonconstant residual gauge function in the ball $\Omega=\{x^2+y^2+z^2<a^2\}$. Apply it to $\phi=0$ and $\mathbf{A}=\tfrac12B_0(-y\hat{\mathbf x}+x\hat{\mathbf y})$, verify Coulomb gauge and both fields directly, and give the relevant SI dimensions and a limiting check.

The identity $
abla\cdot
abla\chi=
abla^2\chi$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Take the divergence of the transformed vector potential before making any topological claim. Treat time as a parameter and use an energy integral to establish boundary-based uniqueness. To disprove uniqueness without boundary data, use a spatially linear harmonic function in a ball and pair its time derivative with the scalar-potential transformation.

milestones.criterion: Derives the residual equation $\nabla^2\chi=0$ by requiring both vector potentials to satisfy Coulomb gauge.
